title: Public-Key Cryptography and RSA
notes: Formula-heavy with a toy worked example (p=3, q=11). The numbers must be reproduced exactly. The lecture explicitly says the toy primes are insecure; dropping that is a faithfulness slip. Traps: elliptic curves, padding schemes and named key sizes the lecture does not give.

pages.text:
Week 9 — Public-Key Cryptography.

Symmetric encryption uses one shared secret key. Public-key encryption uses a pair: a public key to encrypt, a private key to decrypt. Anyone can encrypt to you; only you can decrypt.

RSA security rests on the difficulty of factoring a large number n = p * q into its primes.

Key generation: pick primes p and q, compute n = p * q and phi = (p-1)(q-1). Pick e coprime to phi. Compute d with e * d ≡ 1 (mod phi). Public key (n, e), private key (n, d).

Encrypt: c = m^e mod n. Decrypt: m = c^d mod n.
Toy example, far too small to be secure: p = 3, q = 11, n = 33, phi = 20, e = 3, d = 7 since 3 * 7 = 21 ≡ 1 (mod 20). Encrypt m = 4: c = 4^3 mod 33 = 31. Decrypt: 31^7 mod 33 = 4.
